newsitem.title: USA: U.S. doctors hold out hope for arthritis sufferers.
newsitem.headline: U.S. doctors hold out hope for arthritis sufferers.

text.p: A drug has been developed that researchers believe fights arthritis effectively and protects patients from the potentially life-threatening side effects of current treatments, experts said.

They also told a media briefing in New York that doctors were encouraged by promising research in a separate new class of medications called "cyclo-oxygenase inhibitors" that indicated a potential breakthrough in arthritis therapy.

"The data suggests that we have on the horizon the potential for some really exciting therapy," said Peter Isakson, project director of inflammatory disease research at Searle, the Illinois company that worked on the first product, which is called Arthotec.

Information on Arthotec was presented last week at the European League Against Rheumatism in Madrid, Spain. The second product would be discussed at the annual meeting of the American College of Rheumatology in Orlando on Oct. 18 to 22, the researchers said.
They said Arthotec combines diclofenac, the most widely used non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, and misoprostol, which is used for treating and preventing gastric ulcers.

"This is really a very important area to be able to figure out ways to make people better and we don't yet have cures for these diseases (arthritis)," said Dr. Lee Simon, associate professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School.

The non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, or NSAIDs, are the most widely prescribed medications for arthritis and pain. They relieve arthritis symptoms but carry the risk of gastrointestinal side effects and impair ability of the blood to clot, which are both potentially life-threatening.

An estimated 40 million Americans suffer from arthritis and the number is expected to rise as the population ages. The most common forms are osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis. An estimated 30 million people worldwide rely on daily doses of NSAIDs to relieve their arthritis symptoms.

Simon said arthritis costs the U.S. economy $57 billion a year in lost work time when one considers related complications, the cost of drugs and the toxic nature of the drugs, the use of medications and doctors visits.

Arthotec is already available in 27 countries and Searle has applied to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to approve it. Simon said he hoped it would be approved in "a lot sooner than a year or two years."
